entities.summary:
The Abbasid Caliphate (750–1258 CE) was the third Islamic caliphate, founded when the Abbasid clan overthrew the Umayyad Caliphate in the Abbasid Revolution. Based in Baghdad — the city they built from scratch in 762 CE as a circular planned capital — the Abbasids presided over the Islamic Golden Age, a period of extraordinary scientific, mathematical, literary, and philosophical achievement.

The Abbasid caliphs, particularly Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, patronized the translation movement that preserved and expanded Greek philosophy, mathematics, and medicine. The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad became the world's preeminent intellectual center, where scholars from across the known world translated Aristotle, Plato, Galen, and Euclid while making original contributions. Al-Khwarizmi developed algebra here; al-Biruni pioneered scientific method; al-Kindi explored music theory and optics.

The Mongol invasion of 1258, when Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad and executed the last caliph al-Musta'sim, ended the political Abbasid caliphate and is traditionally regarded as ending the Islamic Golden Age. The destruction of Baghdad's libraries — with books thrown into the Tigris until the river ran black with ink — was one of history's greatest cultural catastrophes. A shadow Abbasid caliphate survived in Cairo under Mamluk patronage until 1517.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Abbasid Caliphate's Golden Age preserved and expanded human knowledge when Europe lay in darkness, transmitting science, philosophy, and mathematics that directly enabled the European Renaissance.
